questions.text: The Gibbs free energy and Helmholtz free energy are defined respectively as:
questions.detailed: $G\equiv H-TS$ and $A\equiv U-TS$. Both subtract the "bound" energy $TS$ from an energy function, leaving the part available to do useful work at constant $T$.

questions.text: At constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous when:
questions.detailed: At constant $T$ and $P$ the system minimises $G$, so a spontaneous change has $\Delta G<0$. At equilibrium $\Delta G=0$.

questions.text: The fundamental differential of the Gibbs free energy is:
questions.detailed: From $G=H-TS=U+PV-TS$ and $dU=T\,dS-P\,dV$, substitution gives $dG=V\,dP-S\,dT$. Its natural variables are $P$ and $T$.

questions.text: Which Maxwell relation follows from $dG = V\,dP - S\,dT$?
questions.detailed: Because $dG$ is exact, the cross-derivatives must match: $\partial V/\partial T|_P = -\partial S/\partial P|_T$. So $(\partial S/\partial P)_T=-(\partial V/\partial T)_P$.

questions.text: The Maxwell relation obtained from $dA=-P\,dV-S\,dT$ is:
questions.detailed: For $dA$ the cross-derivative equality gives $(\partial S/\partial V)_T=(\partial P/\partial T)_V$. This relation is used, for example, to compute entropy changes from $P$–$V$–$T$ data.

questions.text: The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation in its commonly used form is:
questions.detailed: Gibbs–Helmholtz: $\Delta G=\Delta H+T(\partial\Delta G/\partial T)_P$. Equivalently $\partial(G/T)/\partial T|_P=-H/T^2$. It links the temperature slope of $G$ to the enthalpy — essential for extrapolating free-energy data (as on Ellingham diagrams).

questions.text: For a reaction with $\Delta H=-100\ \mathrm{kJ}$ and $\Delta S=-200\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ at $300\ \mathrm{K}$, $\Delta G$ is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S=-100{,}000-300(-200)=-100{,}000+60{,}000=-40{,}000\ \mathrm{J}=-40\ \mathrm{kJ}$. Spontaneous at this temperature.

questions.text: A reaction has $\Delta H=+50\ \mathrm{kJ}$ and $\Delta S=+100\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. It becomes spontaneous above a temperature of:
questions.detailed: Set $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S=0\Rightarrow T=\Delta H/\Delta S=50{,}000/100=500\ \mathrm{K}$. Above 500 K the $-T\Delta S$ term outweighs the positive enthalpy, so the reaction turns spontaneous (e.g. many high-temperature reductions).

questions.text: At the equilibrium temperature of a phase transition, $\Delta G$ equals:
questions.detailed: Two phases coexist in equilibrium when their molar Gibbs energies are equal, so $\Delta G_{\text{trans}}=0$. Hence $\Delta H_{\text{trans}}=T_{\text{trans}}\Delta S_{\text{trans}}$, the basis of the Clapeyron equation.

questions.text: For an ideal-gas phase, the variation of molar Gibbs energy with pressure at constant $T$ is:
questions.detailed: Integrating $dG=V\,dP$ with $V=RT/P$ gives $G=G^\circ+RT\ln(P/P^\circ)$. Pressure raises $G$ logarithmically — the origin of fugacity and of the $RT\ln Q$ term in $\Delta G$.

questions.text: Which partial derivative gives the entropy directly from the Gibbs energy?
questions.detailed: From $dG=V\,dP-S\,dT$, holding $P$ constant gives $(\partial G/\partial T)_P=-S$. Similarly $(\partial G/\partial P)_T=V$.

questions.text: The standard Gibbs energy of formation of an element in its standard state is:
questions.detailed: Like $\Delta H_f^\circ$, the value $\Delta G_f^\circ=0$ for an element in its standard state (the reference). This lets reaction $\Delta G^\circ$ be built from compound data by Hess-type sums.

questions.text: $1$ mol of an ideal gas is compressed isothermally at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ from $1$ atm to $10$ atm. The change in Gibbs energy is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta G=nRT\ln(P_2/P_1)=1\times8.314\times300\times\ln10=2494\times2.303\approx+5740\ \mathrm{J}=+5.74\ \mathrm{kJ}$. Compressing raises $G$; spontaneous expansion would lower it.

questions.text: The four thermodynamic potentials $U,H,A,G$ are related by Legendre transforms. Which gives $A$ from $U$?
questions.detailed: $A=U-TS$ (Helmholtz). Its natural variables are $V,T$. The chain is $U\to A$ (subtract $TS$) $\to G$ (add $PV$), or $U\to H$ (add $PV$) $\to G$ (subtract $TS$).

questions.text: Regarding the sign of $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$, which are correct?

statements.text: If $\Delta H<0$ and $\Delta S>0$, the reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures.
If $\Delta H>0$ and $\Delta S<0$, it is never spontaneous.
If $\Delta H>0$ and $\Delta S>0$, it can become spontaneous at high temperature.

questions.detailed: All three are standard cases. (I) both terms favour reaction; (II) both oppose; (III) the favourable $T\Delta S$ term eventually dominates at high $T$ — the reason many endothermic metallurgical reductions need high temperature.

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.assertion: A reaction with $\Delta H>0$ can still be spontaneous.
questions.reason: The entropy term $-T\Delta S$ in $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$ can outweigh a positive enthalpy.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: Endothermic reactions (e.g. the Boudouard reaction $\mathrm{C+CO_2\to2CO}$, $\Delta H>0$) do become spontaneous at high $T$. The reason is exactly the $-T\Delta S$ term, so R explains A.

questions.text: Given $\Delta G^\circ=-20\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at $298\ \mathrm{K}$, the equilibrium constant $K$ is about ($R=8.314$):
questions.detailed: $\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K\Rightarrow \ln K=20{,}000/(8.314\times298)=8.07\Rightarrow K=e^{8.07}\approx3.2\times10^3$. Negative $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K\gg1$.

questions.text: The relation between $\Delta G$ and $\Delta A$ for a process is:
questions.detailed: From $G=A+PV$, $\Delta G=\Delta A+\Delta(PV)$. For ideal-gas reactions $\Delta(PV)=\Delta n_{\text{gas}}RT$, giving the familiar conversion between free-energy changes at constant $V$ and constant $P$.

questions.text: The condition for equilibrium at constant $T$ and $P$ in terms of the Gibbs energy is:
questions.detailed: At fixed $T,P$ the equilibrium state is the one of minimum $G$, so $dG=0$ (and $d^2G>0$) at equilibrium. Spontaneous change always lowers $G$ until it can fall no further.

questions.text: For a solid that melts, $\Delta S_{\text{fus}}=+30\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$ and $\Delta H_{\text{fus}}=+8{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The melting temperature is:
questions.detailed: At melting $\Delta G=0$, so $T_m=\Delta H_{\text{fus}}/\Delta S_{\text{fus}}=8000/30\approx267\ \mathrm{K}$. Below $T_m$ the solid is stable; above it the liquid is.

questions.text: Which statement about the Gibbs energy is correct?

options.label: b
options.text: It is an extensive state function, and $\Delta G$ is path-independent

options.label: c
options.text: Its value is independent of pressure

questions.detailed: $G$ is an extensive state function (scales with amount, depends only on state). $\Delta G$ between two states is path-independent, and at constant $P$, $\Delta G$ measures the maximum non-$PV$ (useful) work obtainable.

questions.text: The free-energy function method expresses $\Delta G^\circ_T$ using tabulated values of $(G^\circ_T-H^\circ_{298})/T$. This is useful because it:

options.label: a
options.text: Avoids needing heat capacities at every temperature

options.label: d
options.text: Eliminates the need for enthalpy data

questions.detailed: Free-energy functions $(G^\circ_T-H^\circ_{298})/T$ are tabulated once from thermal data, letting $\Delta G^\circ_T=\Delta H^\circ_{298}+T\sum(\text{fef})$ be assembled at any $T$ without re-integrating $C_P$. — a workhorse for compiling Ellingham data.

questions.text: For an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas into a larger volume, $\Delta G$:
questions.detailed: $\Delta G=nRT\ln(P_2/P_1)$; expansion lowers pressure, so $P_2<P_1$, $\ln<0$, giving $\Delta G<0$ — consistent with expansion being spontaneous for an ideal gas into vacuum.

questions.text: "A negative $\Delta H$ always guarantees a spontaneous reaction."
questions.detailed: False. Spontaneity requires $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S<0$. If $\Delta S<0$, a negative $\Delta H$ may still give $\Delta G>0$ at high temperature (the white→grey tin example).

questions.text: Using the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation, if $\Delta G$ at two nearby temperatures changes by $\Delta(\Delta G)$ over $\Delta T$, the reaction enthalpy is best estimated from:
questions.detailed: Gibbs–Helmholtz rearranged: $\Delta H=\Delta G-T(\partial\Delta G/\partial T)_P$. So the temperature slope of $\Delta G$ gives the enthalpy — you can read $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ straight off a plot of $\Delta G$ vs $T$.

questions.text: Match the thermodynamic potential (List I) with its natural variables (List II):
questions.detailed: $U(S,V)$, $H(S,P)$, $A(T,V)$, $G(T,P)$ give the pairing P-2, Q-3, R-4, S-1. These natural variables are exactly the ones held constant when the corresponding potential is minimised.

questions.text: The maximum useful (non-$PV$) work obtainable from a process at constant $T$ and $P$ is:
questions.detailed: At constant $T,P$ the usable work is $w_{\text{useful,max}}=-\Delta G$. The rest of the enthalpy ($T\Delta S$) is unavoidably degraded to heat. At constant $T,V$ the corresponding maximum work is $-\Delta A$.

questions.text: Which of these Maxwell relations is correct?
questions.detailed: From $dU=T\,dS-P\,dV$: $(\partial T/\partial V)_S=-(\partial P/\partial S)_V$. The minus sign appears because $dV$ has a negative coefficient in $dU$. For $dH$ the relation is $(\partial T/\partial P)_S=(\partial V/\partial S)_P$.
